title: Symmetry is the adversary
summary: Identical agents running the same deterministic program can be kept in lockstep forever. Across graphs, the plane and programmable matter, the papers break this symmetry with identifiers, with randomness, with asymmetric starts, or with the scheduler, and leader election keeps reappearing as the common core.

sections.heading: Why identical agents get stuck
sections.body:
Pelc's survey of deterministic rendezvous names the obstacle directly: "The main problem that has to be solved in order to make deterministic rendezvous possible, both in networks and in the plane, is breaking symmetry" [Pelc2019Survey]. His example is an oriented ring, port 0 clockwise at every node, with two identical agents that start at the same time: whatever one does, the other does too, so the distance between them never changes. The same holds in the empty plane for agents with the same compass, unit and speed [Pelc2019Survey]. Ta-Shma and Zwick make the same point when they give their rendezvous agents labels: without them "the rendezvous problem cannot be solved deterministically" [TaShma2014Deterministic].

The argument travels to every model in the catalogue. For dispersion, Das, Bose and Sau spell it out: anonymous agents that start on one node are in the same state and run the same algorithm, so "they will always mirror each other's move" and never separate; the same reasoning gives the $\Omega(\log k)$ bits per agent, for $k$ agents, that every deterministic dispersion algorithm needs [Das2021MemoryOptimal] [Augustine2018Tradeoffs]. In the plane, two oblivious robots cannot gather under a semi-synchronous scheduler [Flocchini2016Constant] (first shown by Suzuki and Yamashita [Suzuki1999Formation], as the catalogue records it), and scattering robots that may start on a common point has no deterministic solution [Dieudonne2009Scatter]. Clement, Défago, Potop-Butucaru, Izumi and Messika put it generally: because robots are anonymous, "the impossibility results proved in classical distributed computing also hold in robot networks", and flocking, gathering or scattering are impossible without additional assumptions [Clement2010Cost].

sections.heading: Which configurations are symmetric
sections.body:
Each model has its own notion of symmetry, and the strongest results characterise it exactly. In port-labelled graphs the notion is the *view* of a node, the infinite tree of port sequences seen from it (introduced by Yamashita and Kameda, as recounted by [Pelc2019Survey]). Two anonymous agents can meet if and only if their starting nodes have different views [Czyzowicz2012Forget], as stated in [Pelc2019Survey]. For larger anonymous teams the asymmetry may come from the agents' positions relative to each other rather than from the graph, which Pelc singles out as the main difficulty solved by Dieudonné and Pelc [Dieudonne2016Anonymous] [Pelc2019Survey].

In the plane the notion is geometric. Dieudonné, Levé, Petit and Villain characterise the positions from which disoriented robots can deterministically elect a leader, with and without a common handedness, for every $n > 1$; both characterisations rest on Lyndon words built from the positions [Dieudonne2013Geoleader]. For fat robots, Gan Chaudhuri and Mukhopadhyaya show that a leader can be elected exactly from asymmetric configurations [GanChaudhuri2015Leader].

sections.heading: Leader election as the common core
sections.body:
Dieudonné, Levé, Petit and Villain open their paper with the reason leader election matters: "many problems that are hard to solve become easier to solve with a leader to coordinate the system" [Dieudonne2013Geoleader]. For robots in the plane the link is an equivalence. Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Widmayer showed that $n \ge 3$ robots that cannot elect a leader cannot form arbitrary patterns (as reported by [Dieudonne2013Geoleader]). Dieudonné, Petit and Villain proved the converse in asynchronous systems for $n \ge 4$ with chirality and $n \ge 5$ without [Dieudonne2010Leader]. Cicerone, Di Stefano and Navarra later gave a full characterisation without chirality, arbitrary pattern formation being solvable exactly from leader configurations, and reported that several earlier proofs, including the arXiv version of [Dieudonne2010Leader], are not correct [Cicerone2019Asynchronous].

Programmable matter repeats the pattern. Derakhshandeh et al. motivate leader election by observing that consensus "can easily be solved once the leader election problem can be solved" and that most shape-formation algorithms depend on a seed [Derakhshandeh2015Leader]. Emek, Kutten, Lavi and Moses Jr. call it "an important primitive ... that subsequently breaks symmetry and coordinates the remaining amoebots", and their deterministic algorithm without chirality also makes the particles agree on a handedness [Emek2019Deterministic]. In the agent-based model on graphs, Kshemkalyani, Kumar, Molla and Sharma note that leader election "can also be seen as a form of symmetry breaking" and build minimum spanning trees, independent sets and dominating sets on the elected leader [Kshemkalyani2024AgentLE].

sections.heading: Identifiers, and how many are needed
sections.body:
The first way out is to give agents labels. Pelc lists it first: distinct labels, each known to its owner, make deterministic rendezvous possible in every connected graph, at a cost that grows with the length of the labels [Pelc2019Survey] [Dessmark2006Deterministic]. In dispersion the identifiers are what the memory pays for: the $\Omega(\log k)$ lower bound is the cost of storing a distinct identifier [Kshemkalyani2025Almost].

Between anonymous and fully labelled lies homonymy, which Delporte-Gallet et al. introduced for Byzantine agreement [Delporte2013Homonyms]. Bouzid and Lamani brought it to robots, recalling that sequences of patterns are formable by labelled robots almost without restriction but by anonymous robots only when all patterns have the same symmetricity [Das2015Sequences]; this gap, they write, "illustrates how much anonymity can be a limiting factor" [Bouzid2011Homonyms]. Asahiro and Yamashita treat the number of distinct programs (target functions) as a resource: gathering needs two, and three once a robot may crash [Asahiro2025MAS]. On graphs, Devismes, Dieudonné and Labourel argue that unique labels can be costly to maintain or undesirable for privacy, and that randomised alternatives give no absolute guarantees; they characterise the teams with repeated labels that can gather and gather all of them in time polynomial in the number $n$ of nodes and in $\log\lambda$, where $\lambda$ is the smallest label [Devismes2026Homonymous].

sections.heading: Randomness and the scheduler
sections.body:
The second way out is randomness. Clement et al. remark that work on robot impossibilities had focused on extra assumptions rather than on randomisation [Clement2010Cost]. Scattering is the clean case: no deterministic algorithm exists [Dieudonne2009Scatter], and Bramas and Tixeuil show that, to scatter $n$ robots, $n\log n$ random bits are necessary in total, give a scattering algorithm that uses that many bits and runs in $O(\log\log n)$ rounds without strong multiplicity detection, and prove that no algorithm without strong multiplicity detection runs in constant expected time [Bramas2017RandomBit]. For dispersion, coin flips replace identifiers: anonymous randomised agents disperse with $O(\log\Delta)$ bits on graphs of maximum degree $\Delta$ [Das2021MemoryOptimal], matching the $\Omega(\log\Delta)$ bound of Molla and Moses Jr. [Molla2019Randomness]. The randomised amoebot algorithm of Derakhshandeh et al. elects a leader in expected time linear in the longest boundary [Derakhshandeh2015Leader].

The third way out lives in the scheduler. Under a sequential scheduler, which activates one robot per round, robots can break symmetry and elect a leader. Flocchini, Navarra, Pattanayak, Piselli and Santoro show that this power is "much stronger than the obvious capacity these schedulers offer of breaking symmetry": every pattern except a point becomes formable from every start, which is impossible under the fully synchronous scheduler even for robots with a leader [Flocchini2026Universal].

sections.heading: What remains open
sections.body: The cost of breaking symmetry is not settled even in the problems that are otherwise solved. Deterministic dispersion runs in optimal $O(k)$ rounds, but with $O(\log(k+\Delta))$ bits; whether $O(\log k)$ bits, the price of an identifier, suffice is open [Kshemkalyani2025Almost]. Anonymous randomised agents disperse with optimal memory, but in $\Theta(k^2)$ rounds against an $\Omega(k)$ lower bound [Das2021MemoryOptimal]. Whether anonymous randomised agents can disperse from an arbitrary configuration and then stop, rather than stay active forever, is open [Molla2019Randomness] [Das2021MemoryOptimal]. And faults bring indistinguishability back: weak Byzantine agents can behave exactly like honest ones and occupy nodes, which makes balanced dispersion impossible whenever $\lceil k/n\rceil > \lceil (k-f)/n\rceil$ [Molla2021ByzantineGraphs].
